title: AEMT Series — Preparatory
notice: PHASE 1 ENGINE SEED. These blocks and items exist to exercise the renderers, the scheduler and the mastery model. They are not reviewed instructional content and must be replaced before any learner uses this for the exam.

objectives.text: Assess decision-making capacity and execute a refusal
Differentiate scope, standard of care, protocol and credentialing
Apply standard precautions and post-exposure procedure
Identify and order the elements of negligence
Apply mandatory reporting and portable medical orders

blocks.title: Refusals

cold_open.text: Two in the morning, a gas-station parking lot. A 24-year-old with a swollen, obviously broken wrist tells you he is not going anywhere — he cannot afford the bill. He is alert, calm, and answers every question you ask.

screens.body_md:
**Capacity is decision-specific.** It is not a property of the patient, it is a property of *this patient making this decision right now*. The same person can have capacity to refuse a splint and lack it to refuse transport for a head injury.

You are assessing four things: can he take in the information, hold onto it, weigh it, and tell you what he decided.

**Capacity is not competence.** Competence is a legal status decided by a court. You will never determine competence in the field.

Capacity is a clinical judgement you make at the bedside, and you make it every time someone declines care.

**Oriented ×4 is a screen, not a standard.** A patient can tell you the year, the place, his name and what happened, and still not be able to weigh the risk of walking away from a head bleed.

Ask him to tell you, in his own words, what could happen if he does not go. The answer is the assessment.

blocks.callback_md:
He can refuse — he is alert, he understands the risk, and he can tell you what he is giving up. What you owe him is a clear explanation of what could go wrong, a repeated offer, and a record that shows both.

**Cost is not incapacity.** A patient refusing for a reason you would not choose is still refusing with capacity.

blocks.title: Integration scenario

cold_open.text: Chest pain, a capable patient, and a family member who disagrees.

blocks.callback_md: Capacity decides. Document what you explained and why you found her capable.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: A 24-year-old who is alert, knows where he is, and can explain the risk of not being transported wants to sign a refusal. What does his ability to explain the risk establish?

options.text: That he has decision-making capacity for this decision
options.rationale: Capacity is decision-specific and rests on understanding the risks, benefits and alternatives — not on orientation alone.
Orientation is a screening observation, not the capacity standard. A patient can be oriented ×4 and still lack capacity.
Competence is a legal determination made by a court. Prehospital providers assess capacity, not competence.

options.text: That medical control need not be contacted
options.rationale: Whether to contact medical control is a protocol question, independent of the capacity finding.

items.explanation_md: Capacity is decision-specific and is assessed at the bedside; competence is a court finding. Orientation ×4 screens but does not establish capacity.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Which term names the range of skills an AEMT is legally permitted to perform in a given state?

options.rationale: Scope of practice is the legally defined set of skills for a licensure level in that jurisdiction.
Standard of care is what a reasonable provider of the same level would do in the same situation — a negligence concept, not a permission list.
A protocol is the medical director’s written instruction. It operates inside scope, it does not define it.
Credentialing is an agency verifying an individual may practice there. It does not set the state scope.

items.explanation_md: Scope is set by the state; protocol is set by the medical director inside that scope; credentialing is the agency permitting an individual to work.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: The 2018 EMS fatigue evidence-based guidelines recommend limiting shift length to less than how many hours?

options.rationale: The guideline panel recommended shifts shorter than 24 hours.
No recommendation was made at 8 hours; the panel addressed the 24-hour threshold.
12 hours is a common scheduling practice but is not the guideline threshold.
48 hours is longer than the threshold the panel recommended against.

items.explanation_md: One of five GRADE-based recommendations: use fatigue survey instruments, shifts under 24 hours, caffeine access, on-duty napping, and fatigue training.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Select all situations in which consent may be implied.

options.text: An unresponsive patient with an obstructed airway
options.rationale: Implied consent covers an emergency in a patient who cannot consent.

options.text: A patient found seizing and unable to communicate
options.rationale: Same basis: an emergency plus an inability to give expressed consent.

options.text: An alert adult who has declined transport twice
options.rationale: An alert adult with capacity gives or withholds expressed consent; nothing is implied.

options.text: A minor with a parent at the bedside
options.rationale: The parent or guardian consents. Implied consent is not needed.

options.text: A patient asking detailed questions about the medication
options.rationale: A patient able to ask questions is able to give expressed, informed consent.

items.explanation_md: Implied consent rests on two conditions together: a genuine emergency, and a patient unable to give expressed consent.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Select the two precautions that apply to every patient contact regardless of suspected diagnosis.

options.rationale: Hand hygiene is the foundation of standard precautions and applies universally.

options.text: Gloves for contact with blood or body fluids
options.rationale: Barrier protection against blood and body fluids is part of standard precautions.
Respirators are selected by exposure risk, not worn for every contact.
That is a facility engineering control, not a prehospital standard precaution.
Sterile technique is procedure-specific and is not a standard precaution.

items.explanation_md: Standard precautions are applied to all patients. Transmission-based precautions are added by suspected route.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Place the four elements of negligence in the order a plaintiff must establish them.

options.rationale: First: a duty must exist before it can be breached.
Second: the provider failed to meet the standard of care.
Third: the patient suffered a compensable harm.
Fourth: the breach must be shown to have caused the damages.

items.explanation_md: Duty → breach → damages → proximate cause. All four must be established; failing any one defeats the claim.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Order the immediate actions after a needlestick from a patient IV start.

options.text: Wash the site with soap and water
options.rationale: Immediate decontamination of the site comes first.
Notification starts the exposure control process and the clock.
Documentation follows notification.

options.text: Present for medical evaluation and follow-up
options.rationale: Evaluation and any prophylaxis follow the report.

items.explanation_md: Decontaminate, notify, document, then evaluate. Sequence matters both clinically and for the employer’s obligations under the exposure control plan.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Sort each situation into the kind of consent it represents.

options.text: An alert adult says "yes, take me in"
options.rationale: Stated agreement is expressed consent.

options.text: A patient holds out an arm for a blood draw
options.rationale: Non-verbal but deliberate agreement is still expressed.
Emergency plus inability to consent — implied.

options.text: A patient who is postictal and not answering
options.rationale: Same basis — implied consent while unable to communicate.

items.explanation_md: Expressed consent is given, verbally or by clear action. Implied consent is supplied by law when an emergency meets an inability to consent.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Sort each skill by whether it is within the Kansas AEMT scope.

options.rationale: IV access is an AEMT skill.
Supraglottic airways are within the AEMT scope.

options.text: Cardiac rhythm interpretation and manual defibrillation
options.rationale: Manual defibrillation and rhythm interpretation are paramedic-level.
Needle decompression is a paramedic skill.

items.explanation_md: SEED PLACEHOLDER — real scope items must be sourced to the National EMS Scope of Practice Model and the current Kansas scope in the local overlay.

items.stem: For each situation, choose whether it triggers a mandatory report.

rows.label: An adult who declines transport for chest pain

items.explanation_md: Mandatory reporting categories are set by state statute. A capable adult refusing care is documented, not reported.

stimulus.alt: Placeholder diagram of a portable medical order form with sections A through D marked.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Section A of this form is left completely blank. What does that indicate?

options.rationale: On the TPOPP form, a section left blank indicates default treatment for that section.
A blank section does not invalidate the form; the rest of the form stands.
Comfort-measures-only must be affirmatively marked, not inferred from a blank.
Declining is not recorded by leaving a section blank.

items.explanation_md: A blank section means full/default treatment for that section — the form never reads a blank as a limitation.

stimulus.text: You are called for a 68-year-old with crushing chest pain. She is alert, answers every question appropriately, and tells you she understands she could die without treatment. She refuses transport. Her daughter is shouting at you to "just take her."

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Who decides whether this patient is transported?

options.rationale: An adult with decision-making capacity decides, regardless of family objection.
Family cannot override a capable adult patient.
Police do not have authority to compel transport of a capable adult on medical grounds.
The hospital has no role in a prehospital refusal decision.

items.explanation_md: Capacity, not diagnosis or family pressure, determines who decides.

items.source_ref: SEED — not for instruction. Replace before publish.
items.stem: Select everything that must appear in your documentation of this refusal.

options.text: The specific risks you explained, in your own words
options.rationale: The record must show what the patient was told.
The capacity finding has to be supported by what you observed.

options.text: That you offered transport again before leaving
options.rationale: A repeated offer is a standard element of a defensible refusal.

options.text: The daughter’s opinion of the decision
options.rationale: A family member’s opinion is not an element of the refusal record.

options.text: A diagnosis of the chest pain
options.rationale: Prehospital providers document findings and impressions, not diagnoses, and a diagnosis is not a refusal element.

items.explanation_md: A defensible refusal records the risks explained, the basis for the capacity finding, and the repeated offer of care.
